articles.title: South Korea, Ukraine relations sour over North Korean POW transfer
articles.body:
South Korea, Ukraine relations sour over North Korean POW transfer
South Korea’s presidential office criticises Ukraine for denying POW nondisclosure agreement.
The South Korean president’s office has expressed “strong regret” over Ukraine’s disregard for a nondisclosure agreement with Seoul in the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul, South Korean media reported.
Last week, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) that his country transferred two North Korean POWs to South Korea.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent two North Korean POWs to South Korea
- list 3 of 3Ukraine’s Zelenskyy calls for sustained pressure to end ‘Putin’s crazy war’
President Lee Jae Myung’s office “expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure [of the transfer] and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement”, the Yonhap news agency quoted Seong Ghi-hong, South Korea’s senior presidential secretary for public relations, as saying in a statement on Sunday.
The office said the nondisclosure agreement aimed to safeguard the soldiers from dangers they could face if their transfer were to be disclosed, in accordance with international law and humanitarian principles.
According to Yonhap, a South Korean media outlet, the Ukrainian presidential office said it had disclosed the transfer of the POWs without extensive details on the process, claiming that it would have been strange to keep the entire transfer a secret. Ukrainian media outlets reported a Ukrainian presidential source as denying the existence of a confidentiality agreement with Seoul, Yonhap said.
The South Korean presidential office said the Ukrainian presidential office’s “false” denial of the confidentiality agreement “seriously hampers” bilateral trust and causes serious disruptions to bilateral friendship.
Seong Ghi-hong said the government was considering additional measures over the issue, if necessary, Yonhap added.
North Korean POWS
Ukrainian forces captured the two North Korean soldiers in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025.
Mounting evidence, including from intelligence reports and testimonies of defectors, has indicated that North Korean soldiers resorted to self-detonation or other forms of suicide rather than be captured.
In his UN address, Zelenskyy said, “These guys are not easy to capture alive.” He added, “One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die.”
South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
The issue of North Korean prisoners of war was a key topic during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkiye, where Lee met Zelenskyy in July.
Senior presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung stated afterwards that both leaders agreed to resolve the status of North Korean POWs in accordance with international law. This built on a prior agreement reached during the South Korea-Ukraine foreign ministers’ meeting in March, where both nations pledged to cooperate on the POW issue.
According to South Korean intelligence, North Korea is estimated to have deployed approximately 14,000-15,000 soldiers to support Russia’s efforts in its war with Ukraine since 2024, primarily in the Kursk border region. South Korean, Ukrainian and Western officials said they suffered heavy casualties, with more than 6,000 North Korean soldiers killed in the fighting.
The transfer comes as South Korea has backed efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, while United States President Donald Trump has renewed his willingness to engage with Pyongyang.

articles.title: Russian drones, missiles continue to batter Kyiv for fourth consecutive night of strikes
articles.body:
9 injured as Russian drones, missiles continue to batter Kyiv for fourth consecutive night of strikes
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russian forces continued to pummel Kyiv with drones, injuring nine, as a multi-day attack stretched into its fourth consecutive night on Sept. 27-28.
Over central Kyiv, air defense systems were reported to be active, filling the city with sounds of blasts and explosions. Nine people were injured in the attacks, said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Six of the injured were hospitalized, including one child.
 A Russian drone was shot down by the capital's air defenses and crashed in the Podil neighborhood, according to eyewitness reports by the Kyiv Independent staff.
"In the Podilskyi district, a fire broke out in the grass cover as a result of falling debris," said Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Emergency services were deployed to the scene.
Debris fell in an open area in the Dnipro district, as well as on a non-residential building, Klitschko said, with preliminary reports indicating that there are casualties.
In the Darnitsky district, debris fell in an open area near a store.
According to Kyiv Independent staff, police halted trains set to depart during the attack, evacuating passengers to underground shelters.
The latest strikes come after days of nearly unrelenting attacks on the capital.
On the night of Sept. 26-27, Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one and injured at least five.
Across Ukraine on Sept. 26-27, attacks by Russian forces killed 14 and injured at least 57.
"This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has effectively abandoned Saudi Arabia, a key ally in the Middle East, leaving it to face “almost a full-blown war” with Yemen’s Houthis, political scientist and University of Chicago Professor John Mearsheimer said in an interview with RT.
Hostilities between Riyadh and the Shiite militant group, officially known as Ansarullah, have flared up in recent weeks after several years of relative calm. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, while Riyadh-backed government forces have tried to hold off the group’s advances inside Yemen.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on for oil exports since navigation through the Strait of Hormuz was reduced to a trickle amid the US-Israeli war against Iran.
In an interview with New Order host Afshin Rattansi on Sunday, Mearsheimer said that because of its “foolish” decision to “attack the Houthis and pick a fight with them,” Saudi Arabia has found itself in “really deep trouble.” He added that the “Houthis are a formidable fighting force, and the Saudis are not.”
He went on to suggest, citing media reports, that Trump encouraged Riyadh to strike an airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in mid-July. The attack, which was apparently meant to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing, shattered the UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis, triggering the current escalation.
Mearsheimer gave credence to claims made earlier this month by the New York Times, which said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned Trump on multiple occasions in recent weeks, asking for military support against the Houthis. The president decided, however, not to intervene, according to the NYT. 
Trump was reportedly close to authorizing strikes on the Houthis last weekend, but reversed his decision at the last minute.
According to Mearsheimer, “the last thing [Trump] wants to do is get into a fight with [the Houthis] to try to rescue Saudi Arabia” – not least because of how badly America’s attempt to bomb the Houthis into submission went last year.
Less than two months into the campaign, Trump abruptly announced a ceasefire, declaring victory and saying the Houthis promised not to attack US ships.
“But in fact, the Houthis beat the United States. We did not defeat the Houthis,” Mearsheimer said.
Speaking to Al-Mayadeen on Saturday, the head of the National Security Committee in the Iranian Parliament, Ibrahim Azizi, warned neighboring Arab nations against cooperating with the US and allowing it to use their territory as a launchpad for attacks.
Azizi added that the US security umbrella in the Middle East has proven to be ineffective.

articles.title: Lavrov dismantles Western narratives at UN, brings West back to reality — diplomat
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 27. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov brought the Western minority back to reality regarding the situation around Ukraine during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, dismantling all of its narratives, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told Vesti.
"This was Sergey Lavrov bringing this Western minority back to reality," she said. "This was particularly evident during the Security Council meeting devoted to the situation around Ukraine. And, of course, at the General Assembly - it was a return to the historical context, to the course of history," the diplomat added.
Zakharova noted that Western representatives take historical episodes out of whichever era and context suits them and begin reshaping them to serve their own immediate interests. "These narratives of theirs were completely dismantled by bringing the discussion back into its historical context and reminding everyone who was actually responsible for all of this and who played the leading role - particularly when we talk about the situation around Ukraine - and what needs to be done to find a way out of it," she added.

articles.title: Hezbollah as we know it died with Nasrallah, now Iran is making the decisions for the Lebanese terror group - analysis
articles.body:

Hezbollah as we know it died with Nasrallah - analysis
Sources close to Hezbollah say current Secretary-General, Naim Qassem, has failed to fill the void left by his predecessor, with the center of the organization's decision-making coming from Iran
"On the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah Secretary General Hassan Nasrallah, the party has not succeeded in fully overcoming the absence of the man who held its leadership for more than three decades, and who transformed the General Secretariat into a political, organizational, military and popular center of gravity that is difficult to replace."
That's how the prominent Saudi newspaper A-Sharq Al-Awsat described the current state of the Lebanese terror group, exactly two years after Israel eliminated Nasrallah by dropping 84 one-ton bombs on his underground bunker in Beirut's southern suburbs.
Sources close to Hezbollah say that current Secretary-General, Naim Qassem, has failed to fill the void left by his predecessor, while the center of gravity in the organization's decision-making is now coming directly from Iran. And that sums up the entire story.
In his 30-plus years as Hezbollah's leader, Nasrallah was able to transform the Lebanese organization from a small insurgent militia to the biggest non-state armed force in the world. The way he did that was to enjoy the benefits of being the crown jewel of Iran's proxy network in the region, while knowing how to balance between demands from Tehran to engage Israel and domestic political considerations seeking to avoid constant clashes with Israel.
This tightrope act enabled Nasrallah to use billions in Iranian funding to build a massive army, but also to establish a deep state in Lebanon, forcing leader after leader in Beirut to bow down to his will.
But Nasrallah overshadowed not only Lebanon, but the entire region. At one point, Nasrallah was dubbed "the strongest man in Iran", and this was when Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was still alive. That's quite an impressive accomplishment.
Suggested articles
The same cannot be said about Naim Qassem. Unlike his predecessor, who maintained his hold over the Arab world with firebrand speeches every few weeks, Qassem rarely delivers televised speeches and has failed to project the same gravitas as Nasrallah.
In his speech commemorating two years since the killing of Nasrallah, Qassem said "Nasrallah's martyrdom has ensured our survival" (which to some extent is true), and vowed to continue on the path of Jihad, "with Palestine as our compass." If that was said by Nasrallah, someone may have believed it. But in post-Nasrallah Lebanon, there are fewer buyers for such messages.
Today, most Lebanese view Hezbollah as a foreign agent, an Iranian organ seeking to destroy Israel from the north. Nasrallah's source of success was to keep the Iranian influence at bay, thus keeping the appearance of being a Lebanese group. In the wake of his death, Iran has completely taken over, with dozens of operatives actively calling the shots on the ground. Qassem is nothing more than window dressing.

articles.body:

3 people killed and 4 injured in shooting at Michigan strip club, police say
‘An altercation occurred and as a result individuals decided to settle it with gun violence,’ said Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison

Three people were killed and four others were injured when an argument led to gunfire at an after-hours strip club on Sunday morning in Detroit, officials said.
Police responding to the 7.21am shooting on a largely residential street found three men who had been fatally shot, Detroit Police Chief Todd Bettison told reporters at a news conference.
Four more people – two men and two women – were taken in private cars to area hospitals.
All the victims are thought to be in their 20s and 30s, Bettison said.
